s: Part one.
Explicit criteria.
By the end of this part, you'll know why a model flags far too much, the named techniques that fix it, and the tempting fixes that don't.
Let's start with a smoke alarm.
Picture one that goes off every time someone makes toast.
Within a week, somebody pulls the battery out.
Then the real fire comes.
And nothing happens.
Now, does telling that alarm to "be more careful" help?
No.
It does nothing.
What fixes it is telling it what counts as smoke, and what counts as toast.
That's the first failure pattern in this domain.
A model is asked to review or flag things.
It flags far too many.
People stop reading its output.
And then a real problem slips through, precisely because everyone learned to ignore it.
The course has a name for the human side of this.
The car alarm effect.
Or trust collapse.
The practical consequence?
A noisy reviewer is worse than no reviewer.
Because it trains people to look away.
So why does it happen?
You give a model a vague standard.
Something like "flag anything risky."
Or "be thorough and conservative."
The model still has to decide where the line sits.
You didn't draw it, so it draws its own.
And it usually draws a generous one.
So the output catches almost every real issue, and buries them under noise.
Here's the key insight.
This is not a reasoning failure.
The model is correctly answering a question you didn't mean to ask.
Now the technical name.
The problem is low precision with high recall.
Precision is the share of flags that were real.
Recall is the share of real issues that got flagged.
And the cause is an underspecified criterion.
A boundary you left undrawn.
Now the fix, in plain words.
You write down the test you actually apply when you make this call yourself.
You name the things to report.
You name the things to ignore.
And you give the model a place to put the cases it genuinely can't decide.
In exam terms, there are a handful of named techniques.
There are six, so I'll take them one at a time.
One.
Categorical criteria.
You replace a vague adjective with named report categories and named skip categories.
Take an infrastructure review.
The report list might be: public exposure of storage or endpoints.
Wildcard permissions in identity and access management.
And unencrypted data at rest.
The skip list might be: tag naming style.
Formatting the linter already accepts.
And minor reordering.
And each finding comes back as one structured object, with the file, the line, the severity, the issue, and a suggested fix.
Two.
A conjunctive test.
Conjunctive just means every condition must hold.
So instead of "flag potential escalation risk," you write this.
Flag a conversation only if the customer has contacted us two or more times about the same issue, and a promised fix or date has already been missed.
Both must be true.
This turns a judgment into a procedure.
One the model can apply, and you can audit.
Three.
An exclusion list.
A positive definition always leaves near misses ambiguous.
So you name the most common wrong flags outright.
In a contract review, "mutual indemnities" might be the most common false alarm.
And naming it costs you one line.
Four.
Grounding in quotes.
You require the model to quote the passage it relied on, for each finding.
Why does that work?
A model that must reproduce the supporting text can't flag a clause that doesn't exist.
And it can't clear a claim without showing where it found it.
Five.
An abstention channel.
You add a required third outcome, alongside flag and don't flag.
It's usually called needs_human_review.
And you ask the model to name the specific test it couldn't verify.
Anthropic's own guidance on reducing hallucinations says this.
Giving the model permission to say it doesn't know substantially reduces false information.
Architecturally, the course says, treat that bucket as a queue, not a failure.
Why?
Uncertainty that lands in a visible queue can be measured and improved.
Uncertainty hidden inside confident answers can't.
Six.
Permission to find nothing.
You say out loud that an empty result is valid and expected.
Without that sentence, the model feels an implicit pressure to produce at least one finding.
Two smaller moves round this out.
First.
Frame whose side the reviewer is on.
For example, "reviewing on behalf of the supplier."
That decides which way directional tests point.
Second.
Define severity levels with concrete code examples, rather than adjectives.
And for extraction work, the same idea reads like this.
Always extract what is stated.
Never fabricate.
And if a value is absent, it is null, not inferred.
Quick recap before the questions.
Noise comes from a line you never drew.
So name what to report, name what to skip, list the common near misses, demand quotes, give "not sure" a place to go, and say that finding nothing is fine.
Right.
Four practice questions, because they test these moves against each other.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
It's a continuous integration step.
That means an automated check that runs on every code change.
It reviews each Terraform infrastructure plan, with the instruction "be thorough and conservative."
It posts about forty-five comments per pull request.
Almost all of them are on tag naming, and formatting the linter already accepts.
Engineers stopped reading within two weeks.
And a plan that made a storage bucket public got merged.
What is the most effective first change?
Take a second.
The answer.
Replace the instruction with named report and skip categories, with one structured finding per issue.
The course names categorical criteria as the most effective first step for false positives.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: change the words to "be more conservative and only raise what truly matters."
Why?
It's still an adjective with no boundary.
The course example shows exactly this, trimming forty-seven flags to thirty-five, while trust stays at zero.
Wrong: filter on the model's self-reported confidence, above zero point nine.
Why?
That confidence reflects its training data, not your standards.
A confident style nitpick is still noise.
And a genuinely new risk can score lower.
Wrong: lower the sampling temperature.
That's the setting that controls randomness.
Why?
It just makes the same noisy comments repeatable.
Here's a phrase to memorise.
Hold on to this line: determinism is not precision.
Question two.
This one is choose two.
Here's the scenario.
A support agent flags "potential escalation risk."
It flags thirty-eight percent of conversations.
Supervisors can handle about five percent.
And leadership adds a second condition.
Cases the agent is genuinely unsure about must stay visible.
Not silently dropped.
Which two changes?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, a conjunctive test, with a list of near misses not to flag.
Second, a required needs_human_review outcome that names the unverifiable test.
Notice how the second constraint picks the second answer.
The words "must stay visible" point straight at the abstention channel.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep only flags above zero point eight five confidence, and quietly drop the rest.
This is the tempting one.
Why is it wrong?
It fails twice.
Self-reported confidence isn't calibrated to your business standard.
And silently dropping the unsure cases throws away exactly what leadership wanted kept.
Wrong: "be conservative and thorough."
Why?
The two words give no boundary.
And they actually pull in opposite directions.
Wrong: temperature zero.
Why?
Same reason as before.
Determinism is not precision.
Question three.
This is the one that trips people up.
Here's the scenario.
A review bot already uses categorical criteria.
Its security and logic findings are precise.
But its performance category runs a false positive rate above sixty percent.
And developers have started ignoring the whole bot.
Rewriting the performance criteria properly will take weeks.
And trust has to recover this sprint, without losing the security signal.
What do you do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Disable only the performance category.
Write its re-enable date into the prompt.
And leave everything else alone.
The course remedy for a category at roughly sixty percent false positives or higher is exactly that.
The re-enable date works as a forcing function, so the rewrite doesn't get forgotten.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise one global confidence threshold across every category.
Why?
That would mute the real security findings too.
And confidence doesn't measure importance anyway.
Wrong: add "be conservative about performance."
Why?
The noisy category stays noisy.
Wrong: ask developers to ignore performance comments.
Why?
That's how they learn to ignore everything.
It's the trust collapse, already underway.
Think of the kitchen smoke detector again.
You switch off the one that keeps going off for toast.
You stick a note on it saying fix by Friday.
You don't turn down every alarm in the house, including the one in the bedroom that works.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A research system has a verification subagent.
It's told to flag any claim that "may not be adequately supported" by the retrieved sources.
It flags fifty-eight percent of claims.
And most of those are stated almost word for word in a source.
Analysts' hours are limited.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Three parts.
Define "unsupported" as a test.
Require a quoted passage for every decision.
And accept zero flags as valid.
A good test would be this.
A claim is unsupported only if no retrieved source contains a passage stating the claim or its figures.
And the quote requirement means a supported claim can't be flagged without the verifier contradicting its own evidence.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: run the verifier three times, and keep only the claims all three agree are unsupported.
That feels rigorous.
Why is it wrong?
All three runs share the same vague criterion.
They read it the same permissive way.
And they agree.
You triple the cost, and remove few flags.
Wrong: "only flag claims you are highly confident about."
Why?
Self-reported confidence is under the same pressure as the flags.
Wrong: temperature zero.
Why?
It fails again, for the same reason.
So, a quick contrast.
When do you reach for criteria, when for a confidence threshold, and when for temperature?
Criteria fix precision.
Because precision problems are boundary problems.
A confidence threshold sounds similar.
But it measures the model's feeling, not your rules.
And a global one damages the categories that work.
Temperature changes consistency.
Never correctness.
And more runs with the same criterion buy agreement, not accuracy.
We'll meet that last idea again in part six.
Two more distractors to know by sight.
First.
Emphasis.
Capital letters.
And threats, such as "flagging a non-risk is a serious error that will be audited."
None of that supplies boundary information.
The course also warns that aggressive directive language can cause overtriggering on current models.
Second.
A softer version of a vague word is still a vague word.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"What is the most effective first step," for false positives.
That points to categorical criteria.
"Uncertain cases must stay visible."
That points to an abstention channel.
"One category is noisy and the others are fine."
That points to disabling that one category.
"Limited reviewer time."
That tells you precision matters more than recall.
That's part one.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Noise comes from a boundary you never drew.
So draw it, with named tests, an exclusion list, quotes, and a place for "not sure."
Coming up in part two: few-shot examples that improve consistency and quality.
